name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,226

clue.text: Decline to participate in operation with seller

blocks.note: OP is the standard short form of operation, as in a military or surgical op
a tout is someone who sells, often tickets at inflated prices

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to take part in a sales operation.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'with' simply sets the seller beside the operation.
explanation.definitionFit: To opt out is the idiomatic phrasal verb for choosing not to join something.

blocks.note: to protest against something is to raise an objection, a verb
a goal is an aim or purpose, here a noun

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as 'is', linking two meanings that are pronounced differently: ob-JECT the verb and OB-ject the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to voice disapproval; the noun means an aim or purpose someone pursues.

clue.text: Aviator to cheek head of tank group moving north

indicators.note: in a down entry, moving north means reading from the bottom upward, so the whole string runs backwards

blocks.note: taken literally, as the word itself
lip is insolent talk, as is cheek
the first letter of tank
a set is a group of people or things

explanation.surface: A pilot is told to give some lip to the leader of a tank group heading north.
explanation.walkthrough: The little word 'to' is not a link here but part of the wordplay, and the whole string is read from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: A test pilot is a type of aviator who flies new aircraft to evaluate them.

clue.text: Complete roof drainage system without roof!

indicators.note: in a down entry the roof is the top letter, so the drainage system loses its first letter

blocks.note: the channel along a roof edge that carries away rainwater

explanation.surface: An exclamation about installing a full rain gutter on a building that has no roof.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the G from GUTTER leaves UTTER; the second 'roof' is the top of the entry, not the building's.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter as an adjective means absolute or total, as in 'utter nonsense'.

blocks.note: level in the sense of even, with scores tied
the closely mown central area of a cricket ground where the strips for play are prepared

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket is a British bat-and-ball game; its square is the prepared middle of the field, of which each match pitch is one strip.
explanation.definitionFit: Being square means being even or tied; the square is also a named region of a cricket ground.

clue.text: Literary don completely repressing unknown love

indicators.note: to repress is to hold down inside, so 'completely' keeps 'unknown love' within it

blocks.note: quite in its sense of fully or entirely
x is the classic algebraic unknown
love is a zero score in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: An academic is utterly holding back feelings for a mysterious sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like a university lecturer, but here it is the Spanish title Don, as in Don Quixote.
explanation.definitionFit: Don Quixote is the famous title character of Cervantes's novel, a knight of Spanish literature.

clue.text: Rescue vessel finishes off undersea repair work

indicators.note: the finishes of the following words are their final letters, which are kept

blocks.note: the final letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: A salvage boat completes underwater repairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finishes off' reads like a verb meaning completes, but it selects the tail letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Noah's Ark saved the animals and his family from the Flood, making it the archetypal vessel of rescue.

indicators.note: only part of the run of words is used, so the letters sit inside them

blocks.note: spans the end of screen, all of Tom and the start of broke

explanation.surface: Someone asks to hide a screen that a man named Tom partly damaged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partially' looks like it describes how Tom broke the screen, but it points to letters spanning three words.
explanation.definitionFit: To entomb is to place a body in a tomb, which is a way of burying it.

clue.text: Perfect packing list for one travelling light?

definitions.text: packing list for one travelling light?

blocks.note: an idiom for exactly what is needed

blocks.clueFragment: packing list for one travelling light?
blocks.note: read literally, a minimal traveller packs nothing except their fare

explanation.surface: A tip on the ideal packing checklist for a minimalist traveller.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second half is whimsical: the lightest possible luggage is nothing but your ticket.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something exactly right or ideal for the purpose.

indicators.note: the preceding words are altered in form, so their letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder taken as printed

explanation.surface: Visit a sponsor who is switching to a constructed tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like an instruction to the reader, but it is just three letters of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Esperanto was invented by Zamenhof in 1887 as an international auxiliary tongue, so it is constructed rather than natural.

clue.text: Escapade with cloak ending in disaster

indicators.note: the ending of the next word is its final letter

blocks.note: a cape is a sleeveless cloak
the final letter of disaster

explanation.surface: A cloak-and-dagger adventure that ends badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' simply places the cloak before the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A caper is a playful or daring exploit, often a heist, much like an escapade.

clue.text: Investigation admitting large and medium difficulty

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so 'investigation' takes 'large' inside

blocks.note: a probe is an inquiry
L is the clothing size abbreviation
M is the clothing size abbreviation

explanation.surface: An inquiry confesses to a moderately large hitch.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'large' goes inside; 'and medium' is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A problem and a difficulty are straightforward synonyms for a troublesome matter.

indicators.note: something developed has been worked into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder taken as printed

explanation.surface: A car fuelled by an American mine that has been opened up.
explanation.walkthrough: US is taken as printed, two letters of the fodder rather than a country.
explanation.definitionFit: A limousine is a large luxurious car, one example of a motor vehicle.

clue.text: Source of light amber ales going bust

indicators.note: things that go bust break apart, so the letters are scattered and reformed

blocks.note: the fodder taken as printed

explanation.surface: A brewery of pale amber beers is going bankrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light amber ales' pulls 'light' into the beer description, but it belongs with 'Source of'.
explanation.definitionFit: A laser beam is a narrow concentrated ray that supplies intense illumination.

indicators.note: the preceding words are smashed up, so their letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder taken as printed

explanation.surface: Someone watched a plate get smashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' could be a cutting tool, but it is the past tense of see.
explanation.definitionFit: Sighted is the past tense of sight, meaning caught a glimpse of or spotted.

indicators.note: on the radio words are heard, not seen, so the spelling is only by sound

blocks.note: a talk is a lecture; in British speech without a pronounced R the two words sound alike

explanation.surface: A physics broadcast giving a lecture on rotation.
explanation.walkthrough: The match works in non-rhotic accents such as standard British English, where the R in the answer is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: In physics, torque measures the twisting effect that makes an object turn about an axis.

clue.text: Holy book contains introduction from erudite Asian

indicators.note: the holy book holds the next piece inside itself
the introduction of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: the Koran is the holy book of Islam
the first letter of erudite

explanation.surface: A scripture includes a foreword by a learned scholar from Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erudite Asian' reads as one learned person, but 'erudite' only lends its first letter and 'Asian' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A Korean is a person from Korea, a country in East Asia, so an example of an Asian.

indicators.note: going back the way it came means the word is read backwards

blocks.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company
to tag on is to add something at the end

explanation.surface: Guests coming back to join in a gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To add' is taken whole as the phrasal verb TAG ON.
explanation.definitionFit: An octagon is an eight-sided polygon, one specific geometric figure.

blocks.note: Mickey Mouse's pet dog in the cartoons
the dwarf planet beyond Neptune

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as 'is'; 'heavenly body' suggests a glamorous figure, but it is an object in space.
explanation.definitionFit: Pluto is both the cartoon dog of Mickey Mouse and the dwarf planet, formerly counted as the ninth planet.

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two end letters

blocks.note: a pen is an instrument for writing
the first and last letters of nice

explanation.surface: An author enjoying a very pleasant noodle dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely nice' reads as very good, but it keeps only the ends of nice.
explanation.definitionFit: Penne is a kind of short tube-shaped Italian noodle cut on the diagonal.

indicators.note: things upended are knocked over and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder taken as printed

explanation.surface: Questions from the military alliance overturned a review.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enquiries' is a nice red herring, since the answer is itself a set of questions.
explanation.definitionFit: A questionnaire is a printed form of questions used to poll people, the tool of a survey.

indicators.note: only some of the following word is used, so the letters lie within it

blocks.note: the second to fourth letters

explanation.surface: Part of a woven strap is pulling back.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit inside webbing, just after the W.
explanation.definitionFit: The tide ebbs when it flows back out to sea, so to ebb is to draw back or retreat.

indicators.note: moving back means the preceding piece is read in reverse

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as me
a body is an organised group, as in a governing body

explanation.surface: The crossword compiler is personally supporting a band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing group' looks like a band behind a singer, but 'backing' reverses the setter and 'group' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To embody a quality is to give it concrete form, which is what personifying does.

clue.text: River cut off by mouth of Nile

indicators.note: a mouth is where something opens, here the opening letter of the word

blocks.note: to sever is to cut off
the first letter of Nile

explanation.surface: A river blocked off where the Nile meets the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouth of Nile' reads as a delta but gives only a letter; the Severn is Britain's longest river, flowing between England and Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The Severn is a specific British waterway, so an example of the category named.
